facts.text: In October 1997 the Swedish Parliament passed a road traffic safety bill that made Vision Zero the basis of road safety policy.
Vision Zero's long-term goal is that no one should be killed or seriously injured in road traffic.
Vision Zero aims at zero deaths and serious injuries, not zero crashes.
Vision Zero assumes that road users will make mistakes and places responsibility on the people who design and run the road system, who must anticipate those mistakes.
Sweden adopted Vision Zero even though it already had one of the lowest road traffic casualty rates in the world.
Pedestrians usually survive when hit by a car moving below 30 km/h.
Occupants of well-designed cars can tolerate crashes at about 70 km/h head-on and about 50 km/h from the side.
Vision Zero design keeps people on foot away from vehicles faster than 30 km/h and keeps cars from meeting oncoming traffic at high speed.
A meta-analysis of studies found that roundabouts reduced injury crashes by 30 to 50 percent and fatal crashes by 50 to 70 percent.
On 2+1 roads in Sweden, a cable barrier in the middle keeps vehicles from crossing into oncoming traffic and absorbs the energy of a collision.
One meta-analysis found that median cable barriers raised the crash rate by about 30 percent but lowered the chance of fatal injury by about 20 percent.
Norway, the United Kingdom and Canada have built Vision Zero principles into their road safety plans, and many US cities, including New York City, have adopted it.
The World Bank indicator gives estimated road traffic deaths per 100,000 people.

Derived from the dataset: South Korea fell from 25.6 (2000) to 8.6 (2019), about one-third; Norway (2.1) was below Sweden (3.1) in 2019; the US rate rose from 11.7 (2010) to 12.7 (2019); the world fell by 2.4 and Japan by 8.9 between 2000 and 2019.
